mcqs.question: For an operation spanning multiple services that can't share a transaction, what should the API's response design do?
options: Always return a single 500 error if any sub-step fails, to keep the contract simple
Report per-item status in the response, and make each sub-step idempotent so callers can safely retry just the failed parts
Silently retry every failed sub-step server-side until it succeeds, without informing the caller
Require the caller to manually inspect server logs to determine what succeeded
mcqs.explanation: Per-item status tells the caller exactly what happened, and idempotent sub-steps make it safe for them to retry only what failed — together they replace the missing cross-service transaction. A single blanket error hides which parts actually succeeded, silent infinite server-side retries can mask a genuine failure, and requiring log inspection pushes debugging work onto every caller.

mcqs.question: An order's inventory decrement and payment charge succeed, but the loyalty-points award fails because that service is down. Who decides whether the order still counts as placed?
options: The database automatically decides based on which steps succeeded
The business, since "is a half-completed order OK to show as placed" is a product decision, not a purely technical one
Whichever engineer is on call when the failure happens
The payment provider, since they processed the charge
mcqs.explanation: Whether a partially-completed operation counts as a success is fundamentally a product/business call about customer experience, not something to decide ad hoc in code or leave to whoever's on call. Databases don't make business judgments, and the payment provider has no say in your order semantics.

mcqs.question: What does reporting partial success (per-item status) cost the caller, compared to a single success/fail response?
options: It requires the caller to handle a mixed-result response, checking each item's status individually instead of branching on one flag
It makes the API permanently slower, regardless of load
It removes the caller's ability to retry any failed items
It requires the caller to use a different network protocol entirely
mcqs.explanation: Per-item reporting is more honest but genuinely adds caller-side complexity — instead of one branch, the caller has to inspect each item's outcome and act accordingly. It has nothing to do with network protocol or inherent latency, and it actually enables safer retries of failed items rather than removing that ability.

mcqs.question: A caller retries an entire failed batch after a partial failure. Under what condition do the already-succeeded items get duplicated?
options: Only if the API returns a 200 status code instead of a 207
Only if each item's operation isn't idempotent, so repeating it creates a new record instead of recognizing it already happened
Duplication is unavoidable any time a batch request is retried
Only if the batch contains more than 50 items
mcqs.explanation: Duplication on retry happens specifically when an operation lacks idempotency — repeating a non-idempotent create just makes another record. The status code returned and the batch size don't determine whether duplication occurs, and duplication is very much avoidable with proper idempotency keys.
